abstract.p: The prediction of Antimicrobial Peptides (AMPs) is a critical research area in drug discovery. Traditional methods, which rely on sequence alignment or handcrafted features, often fail to capture complex sequence-function relationships. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) like ESM2 have demonstrated remarkable success in extracting deep semantic features from protein sequences. Meanwhile, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly Graph Attention Networks (GATs), can effectively learn inter-node relationships, specifically capturing peptide-residue compositional links and inter-residue co-occurrence patterns, to aggregate neighborhood information. In this work, we propose PepGraphormer, a novel fusion model that combines the powers of large-scale pretraining from ESM2 and the structural learning advantages from GATs for AMP prediction. We first construct a heterogeneous graph with peptide sequences and amino acids as nodes, where ESM2 is leveraged to generate high-quality initial embeddings for the peptide sequence nodes. Then the classification fuses the direct predictions from ESM2 and the graph-based predictions from the GAT. The training jointly trains the ESM2 and GAT modules and learns the embeddings for nodes in the graph. Comparisons with current state-of-the-art models on multiple datasets demonstrate that PepGraphormer achieves excellent accuracy and stability in the AMP prediction task. Further ablation and generalization experiments confirm the effectiveness and robustness of this fusion framework, presenting a new avenue for computationally-driven therapeutic peptide discovery.

Scientific contribution This work proposes a novel framework PepGraphormer that combines the powers of transformer-based large language model (ESM2) and graph attention network for antimicrobial peptide prediction, without requiring the 3D protein structural information used in previous studies. The model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods and various deep learning baselines on multiple AMP benchmark datasets.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Antimicrobial Peptides (AMPs) are a class of biologically active peptides with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, playing a key role in the immune defense of organisms [1, 2]. In the face of the escalating problem of antibiotic resistance, AMPs have become a major research focus thanks to their unique antimicrobial mechanisms, lower risk of inducing drug resistance, and broad specificity [3, 4]. However, traditional discovery methods are complex, costly, and inefficient, failing to meet the urgent demand for novel AMPs [5]. Consequently, researchers have increasingly turned to computational methods [6], with machine learning approaches achieving significant milestones [7]. Early methods often relied on conventional algorithms such as Random Forest (RF) [8–11], Support Vector Machines (SVM) [12–15], and ensemble learning methods [16, 17]. A common limitation of these methods is their reliance on handcrafted features, which requires domain expertise and restricts their universality and scalability.

Deep learning overcomes these limitations by leveraging multi-layer neural network architectures to automatically learn and extract high-level, abstract features from raw sequence data [18–22], significantly advancing the computational prediction of AMPs. This paradigm encompasses various architectures. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [23, 24] excel at capturing local motifs, while Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [25, 26] and their variants like LSTM [27, 28] are used to model sequential context and long-range dependencies. More recently, the Transformer architecture [29], with its self-attention mechanism, and its derivative large language models (such as BERT [30] and ESM [31]) have become the dominant paradigm, establishing a new standard for protein and peptide representation learning and function prediction due to their outstanding sequence modeling capabilities.

Concurrently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex relationships between entities [32]. For instance, LABAMP [33] constructs a graph containing sequence nodes and k-mer nodes (e.g., tripeptides). The framework then leverages a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to learn node representations for identifying bacteriocins. A different and prominent line of work focuses on the internal structure of individual peptides. The sAMPpred-GAT [34] model begins by predicting the contact map of each peptide using trRosetta. It then constructs an individual intra-molecular graph where nodes are amino acids and edges represent their spatial proximity based on the predicted residue distances. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) is then used to learn discriminative features from these structural graphs. Building on this structure-based approach, TP-LMMSG [35] innovates on the node feature representation by employing pre-trained language models. In a separate work, Cordoves-Delgado et al. [36] construct graphs from ESMFold-predicted 3D structures, while leveraging ESM-2 embeddings for amino acid-level features. Similarly, PepTriX [37] employs ESMFold-predicted structures with a GAT enhanced by contrastive training and cross-modal co-attention. However, these structure-based approaches share a common limitation: they require computationally expensive 3D structure prediction as a prerequisite step, and their graph construction is confined to individual peptides without capturing inter-sequence relationships.

In this work, we propose a novel framework PepGraphormer that combines the powers of transformer-based LLMs and GNNs for antimicrobial peptide prediction. Unlike previous GNN-based methods, PepGraphormer bypasses 3D structure prediction entirely, eliminating the substantial computational burden associated with auxiliary folding algorithms and avoiding the inherent noise and bias introduced by the potentially low-confidence structural predictions of short, flexible peptides.. PepGraphormer constructs a single, inter-molecular, heterogeneous graph that covers the entire dataset. In this graph, edges are defined not by physical distance but by statistical relationships: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) [38] for sequence-to-amino-acid edges, and Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) [39] for amino-acid-to-amino-acid edges. PepGraphormer is designed to synergistically leverage the powerful feature extraction capabilities from ESM2 and the relational dependencies learned by a GAT from the graph, aiming to enhance the accuracy and robustness of peptide function prediction. Experimental results show that PepGraphormer outperforms or performs comparably to current SOTA methods on seven benchmark datasets and demonstrates strong generalization to other therapeutic peptide prediction tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lincubator/PepGraphormer.

sec.title: Overview
sec.p:
PepGraphormer integrates a protein language model with a GAT to improve AMP prediction performance. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the process begins with an input peptide sequence, which is encoded by the ESM2 model. The resulting sequence-level feature vector serves a dual purpose: it acts as the initial representation for the corresponding sequence node in the GAT network, and provides a partial prediction based on the sequence information. The GAT operates on a heterogeneous graph composed of sequence nodes and amino acid nodes. It employs a multi-head attention mechanism to learn the importance of neighboring nodes, aggregating feature information from multi-hop neighborhoods to integrate both local context and global structural dependencies. Finally, the model's prediction results from the fusion of ESM2's deep semantic understanding and the GAT's learned relational features. This approach effectively captures amino acid co-occurrence patterns and deep semantic features, thereby improving predictive performance.Fig. 1
Overall Architecture of PepGraphormer. (a) Input: The model takes the amino acid sequence of a peptide as its initial input. (b) Feature Extraction: The ESM2 model extracts deep semantic features from the input sequence. These features serve a dual purpose: they are used directly for an independent AMP prediction branch and also act as the initial embeddings for the sequence nodes in the heterogeneous graph. (c) Graph Construction: A heterogeneous graph, comprising sequence nodes and amino acid nodes, is constructed by combining the raw sequence information with the features generated by ESM2. (d) Graph Learning: The GAT operates on the constructed heterogeneous graph, leveraging its multi-head self-attention mechanism to learn complex intra-sequence and inter-sequence structural dependencies. (e) Fusion and Prediction: Finally, the model fuses the prediction outputs from both the ESM2 and GAT branches to yield the final classification, determining whether the peptide is an AMP or a Non-AMP

This indicates that for this task, the contextual and relational features learned from the graph structure play a critical supplementary role in improving prediction accuracy.

sec.title: Evaluation dataset
sec.p: To ensure an objective evaluation of the model's predictive performance, we not only adopted the datasets previously used by Xu et al. [42], sAMPpred-GAT [34], and TP-LMMSG [35], but also strictly adhered to the data processing protocols established in these benchmark studies to eliminate potential bias.. For these datasets, the positive samples were comprehensively curated from typical AMP databases, including SATPdb [43], ADAM [44], AMPfun [10], APD3 [45], CAMP [46, 47], LAMP [48, 49], DRAMP [50], and dbAMP [51]. The curation process involved removing sequences with non-standard residues and retaining only those with lengths between 11 and 100 amino acids. Furthermore, to mitigate biases from sequence homology and redundancy, CD-HIT [52] was employed to reduce the sequence identity to a 90% threshold [28] both within each dataset and against any positive samples in the independent test sets.

For the negative samples, non-antimicrobial peptide sequences were selected from the UniProt [53] by excluding entries containing keywords such as “antimicrobial” or “antibacterial”. These sequences underwent the same cleaning and length-filtering process. CD-HIT was similarly used to reduce sequence identity to a 40% threshold [28] among the negative samples within each dataset and against the independent test sets. The XUAMP dataset was compiled from the other six datasets. Additionally, to validate the model's ability to generalize to other therapeutic peptides, the imbalanced Antiviral Peptide (AVP) and Anticancer Peptide (ACP) datasets, as compiled in TP-LMMSG [35], were also included in our experiments. For data partitioning, we adopted the same training and independent test set splits as established in prior benchmark studies [34, 35, 42]. sec.title: Evaluation metrics
Performance comparison with other methods
sec.p: To validate the efficacy of PepGraphormer, a systematic evaluation of its performance, robustness, and stability was conducted against several SOTA methods. This comprehensive comparison was conducted across seven independent test sets under strict evaluation criteria established in previous work, with all reported metrics representing the mean and standard deviation of 10 independent runs.

As shown in Table 3, the PepGraphormer model outperforms SOTA methods on the XUAMP independent test set. PepGraphormer ranks first in four core metrics: Accuracy (ACC = 0.7552), Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC = 0.5326), Sensitivity (Sn = 0.6017), and AUC (0.8149). For instance, compared to the high-performing TP-LMMSG model, PepGraphormer shows improvements of 2.14% and 4.66% in ACC and MCC, respectively. The advantage is even more pronounced when compared to sAMPpred-GAT, with improvements of 5.62% and 14.78% in the same metrics. Furthermore, PepGraphormer achieves a strong balance between high recognition capability (high Sn) while maintaining excellent specificity (Sp = 0.9091). Finally, the standard deviation for PepGraphormer is lower than that of other methods across all metrics, which indicates our model's superior stability and consistency. Table 3

For the performance evaluation on the other six datasets, we conducted a comparison against sAMPpred-GAT and TP-LMMSG. These models were selected as they currently represent the top-performing methods on these datasets based on comprehensive performance metrics. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the PepGraphormer model demonstrates the best or nearly the best performance across all six other independent test sets (APD3, DRAMP, LAMP, CAMP, dbAMP, and YADAMP) on three key evaluation metrics: ACC, MCC, and AUC. Notably, even on datasets like DRAMP and LAMP, where the performance of other models is generally lower, PepGraphormer consistently maintains a significant performance advantage. Furthermore, an analysis of the error bars reveals that PepGraphormer exhibits a generally smaller range of performance fluctuation.Fig. 2
Performance comparison of different models across other 6 independent datasets

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of PepGraphormer on the antimicrobial peptide prediction task, we compared it against a diverse set of advanced deep learning baselines. These baselines include language models such as the Transformer model [29], Bert [61], and its variants Bert_CNN [62] and Bert_RNN [63], as well as graph-based models like GIN [64], GraphSAGE [65], and ChebGCN [66]. The performance radar chart in Fig. 3 shows that the red polygon representing the PepGraphormer model is the largest overall, almost completely enveloping the polygons of all other models. This visual dominance clearly indicates that PepGraphormer achieves the most comprehensive and well-balanced lead across the five key evaluation metrics. Specifically, compared to the next-best performing model, Bert_CNN (ACC = 0.698, AUC = 0.738, MCC = 0.414), PepGraphormer shows improvements of 7.55% in ACC, 9.43% in AUC, and 27.92% in MCC, respectively. The model also holds a leading position in both Sensitivity (0.5877) and Specificity (0.9126), demonstrating its ability to effectively identify true antimicrobial peptides while accurately ruling out non-antimicrobial ones.Fig. 3
Radar Chart Comparison of PepGraphormer against Deep Learning Baselines

sec.title: Modal performance verification analysis
sec.p:
To validate the independent contributions of each module and to determine the optimal fusion strategy for the two key components—the ESM2-based prediction and the GAT-based prediction—we designed a series of experiments. In these experiments, we systematically evaluated the model's performance across various metrics while adjusting the fusion factor, m, from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1. The heatmap in Fig. 4 shows that the model's performance does not increase linearly with m. Instead, it exhibits a fluctuating trend, indicating a search for an optimal balance. The columns corresponding to m = 0.8 and m = 0.9 display the highest overall color intensity, forming a “performance hotspot.” For ACC and MCC—often considered the most important and comprehensive metrics for evaluating a classification model—the values at m = 0.8 (0.7559 and 0.5326, respectively) are the highest across all values of m. Therefore, the strong performance of these core metrics at m = 0.8 within the hotspot zone indicates that the model's overall predictive power and balance are optimal at this fusion ratio.Fig. 4
Heatmap of the Impact of Fusion Ratio (m) between ESM2 and GAT on Model Performance

To further validate the indispensable role and critical contribution of each core module within the PepGraphormer architecture, we designed and conducted a series of ablation studies. In these studies, we independently replaced the language model module ESM2 with BERT and the GAT with GCN. These model variants were then evaluated under identical conditions. The experimental results clearly show that replacing any of PepGraphormer's core components leads to a significant decline in the model's overall performance, validating our choice of ESM2 and GAT. When we replaced ESM2 with Bert (BertGAT), the model's ACC dropped substantially from 0.7552 to 0.7010, while the MCC decreased significantly from 0.5326 to 0.4040. This indicates that ESM2 is more effective than Bert in capturing sequence-level semantic information and is a critical component of the model's high performance. Similarly, when GAT was replaced with GCN (ESMGCN), all key metrics showed a comprehensive decline, with AUC dropping from 0.8149 to 0.7765. This suggests that GAT's attention mechanism more effectively aggregates neighborhood information from the graph structure, contributing more to the model's performance than a standard GCN. When both core modules were replaced simultaneously (BERTGCN), its performance was the lowest among all variants. This result serves as further evidence for the “1 + 1 > 2” synergistic effect between the ESM2 and GAT modules in our architecture. In conclusion, this series of ablation studies demonstrates the rationality and effectiveness of the PepGraphormer architecture.

sec.title: Study on model generalization ability
sec.p:
To evaluate the generalization capability of PepGraphormer beyond AMP prediction, we tested its performance on two other therapeutic peptide datasets, ACPs and AVPs, comparing it against state-of-the-art models. As shown in Table 5 and Fig. 5, PepGraphormer demonstrates highly competitive performance on the AVP prediction task. It achieves the top scores in three key metrics: ACC = 0.9777, MCC = 0.9334, and Sp = 0.9905. sec.title: Explainability analysis
sec.p:
To gain deeper insights into the working mechanisms and learning dynamics of the PepGraphormer model, we visualized the feature representations of antimicrobial peptide sequences at various stages of the training process using the t-SNE dimensionality reduction technique. This evolutionary process is illustrated in Fig. 6.Fig. 6
t-SNE visualization of the feature space evolution during the training process of the PepGraphormer model. a Feature Space Distribution of Initial ESM2 Embeddings (Epoch 1–ESM Feature Space). This panel illustrates the distribution of the initial sequence-level embeddings in a 2D t-SNE space. These embeddings are generated by the pre-trained ESM2 model and serve as the initial features before GAT processing. b–f Evolution of the GAT Feature Space During Training (Epochs 1, 11, 21, 31, 51–GAT Feature Space)

As illustrated in Fig. 6a, ESM2, by virtue of its powerful pre-training, can already achieve a certain degree of separation between positive samples (AMPs, blue dots) and negative samples (red dots). This indicates that the initial ESM2 embeddings inherently contain semantic information relevant to AMP function. However, a significant overlap region exists between the two classes, resulting in a fuzzy decision boundary. This suggests that relying solely on ESM2's global semantic features for classification has its limitations. In the initial stage of training (Fig. 6b), the GAT module has just begun to learn. At this point, the feature space distribution of the GAT output shows no clear trend of change compared to the initial ESM2 embedding distribution. This is because the GAT's parameters are not yet sufficiently optimized, and the modifying effect of the graph structural information on the original ESM2 features is still negligible. As training progresses (Figs. 6c–e), a significant improvement in the separability of positive and negative sample points is observed in the t-SNE space. The clusters of antimicrobial and non-antimicrobial peptides begin to form more distinct boundaries, and the overlapping region gradually diminishes. This indicates that the GAT is effectively supplementing and refining the original ESM2 embeddings by aggregating neighborhood information, making the sequence representations more discriminative. In the later stages of training (Fig. 6f), the class separability in the feature space reaches a relatively stable and high level. The positive and negative samples have formed two distinct, concentrated clusters with a clear boundary. This visually demonstrates that the GAT module, by propagating and aggregating information on the heterogeneous graph, has successfully learned feature representations that can better distinguish between the different functional peptide sequences.

This series of t-SNE visualizations provides compelling evidence for the effectiveness of PepGraphormer's hybrid architecture. The evolutionary process of the feature space—from an initial mixed state to a final, clearly separated one—visually demonstrates the critical role that the GAT plays in supplementing ESM2's global features and ultimately enhancing the model's predictive performance.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This paper introduced PepGraphormer, a deep learning framework that integrates the pre-trained protein language model ESM2 with a Graph Attention Network to predict antimicrobial peptides. Evaluations on public datasets show that PepGraphormer holds a significant advantage over other state-of-the-art models. The effectiveness of its dual-modal fusion architecture was validated through comprehensive ablation studies and generalization experiments. By bypassing 3D structure prediction, PepGraphormer offers an efficient framework for peptide function prediction, potentially accelerating the discovery pipeline for new therapeutic peptides. Future work will focus on optimizing the graph construction strategy and exploring more effective data augmentation techniques. We also plan to extend the framework to multi-label classification for predicting specific antimicrobial activities (e.g., antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral), and investigate transfer learning methods tailored for small-sample scenarios to further enhance performance on small-scale or imbalanced datasets.
